Yes, the story has an appropriate and highly effective balance between scene and summary/exposition. 

The writer uses exposition and summary at the beginning to establish the setting, Barbara's condition, and the background of Rabbi Adler, which gives emotional weight to the narrative. As the story reaches its climax in the synagogue, it shifts seamlessly into vivid, real-time scenes—capturing the sensory details of the sanctuary, the stillness of the shooter, the mechanics of the shooting, and the chaotic panic of the crowd. Afterward, the writer returns to summary to compress the passage of time (the birth of the baby, the funeral, and the decades that follow), allowing for a poignant reflection on how that single, dramatized moment affected Barbara for the rest of her life.
